claims.text: Risk beliefs about infectious disease correlate reliably with getting vaccinated.
Anticipated regret about infectious disease correlates reliably with getting vaccinated.
Low confidence in vaccine effectiveness correlates reliably with not getting vaccinated.
Concern about vaccine safety correlates reliably with not getting vaccinated.
Few randomized trials have successfully changed what people think and feel about vaccines.
Randomized trials that successfully changed thoughts and feelings about vaccines were minimally effective in increasing vaccination uptake.
Social norms are associated with vaccination.
Few interventions have examined whether normative messages increase vaccination uptake.
Altruism can affect intended vaccination behavior in experimental studies using hypothetical scenarios.
Free riding can affect intended vaccination behavior in experimental studies using hypothetical scenarios.
Few randomized trials have tested strategies to change social processes to increase vaccination uptake.
Interventions can facilitate vaccination by building on favorable intentions through reminders, prompts, and primes.
Interventions can facilitate vaccination by reducing barriers through logistics and healthy defaults.
Interventions can shape vaccination behavior through incentives, sanctions, and requirements.

evidence.description: Hundreds of studies have shown that risk beliefs about infectious disease correlate reliably with getting vaccinated.
Hundreds of studies have shown that anticipated regret about infectious disease correlates reliably with getting vaccinated.
Hundreds of studies have shown that low confidence in vaccine effectiveness correlates reliably with not getting vaccinated.
Hundreds of studies have shown that concern about safety correlates reliably with not getting vaccinated.
The authors found that few randomized trials have successfully changed what people think and feel about vaccines.
Those few randomized trials that successfully changed thoughts and feelings about vaccines were minimally effective in increasing uptake.
Substantial research has shown that social norms are associated with vaccination.
Few interventions examined whether normative messages increase vaccination uptake.
Many experimental studies have relied on hypothetical scenarios to demonstrate that altruism can affect intended behavior.
Many experimental studies have relied on hypothetical scenarios to demonstrate that free riding can affect intended behavior.
Few randomized trials have tested strategies to change social processes to increase vaccination uptake.
Interventions build on existing favorable intentions by facilitating action through reminders, prompts, and primes.
Interventions build on existing favorable intentions by reducing barriers through logistics and healthy defaults.
Interventions shape vaccination behavior through incentives, sanctions, and requirements.

methodologies.name: Psychological Science Synthesis on Vaccination Uptake
methodologies.description: Reviews and synthesizes empirical studies and randomized trials across three propositions to evaluate psychological mechanisms and interventions for vaccination uptake.

limitations.text: Few randomized trials have successfully changed what people think and feel about vaccines.
Few interventions have examined whether normative messages increase vaccination uptake.
Many experimental studies demonstrating effects of altruism and free riding rely on hypothetical scenarios rather than actual uptake behavior.
Few randomized trials have tested strategies to change social processes to increase vaccination uptake.
Identification of principles for changing thoughts and feelings to motivate vaccination remains a work in progress.

future_work.text: Identify principles for changing thoughts and feelings to motivate vaccination.
Test strategies in randomized trials to examine whether changing social processes increases vaccination uptake.
